note: Ways of getting about for the Draft Table, by era group. `min_hoods`: only in a place with at least this many neighbourhoods; `water`: only where the place has that water; `eras` and `aboard` narrow it further. `speed` is km/h for the city's speeds.

transit.summary: How almost everyone gets about: the town can be walked end to end in half an hour.
Those who can afford it ride; others hire a hackney from the ostlers at the inn.
Ox and horse carts carry goods and anyone willing to sit on the load, leaving from the market on market days.
Barges and rowing boats carrying goods and passengers along the water for a penny.
A rope ferry across the water, for when the bridge is too far or the ford too high.
Most people walk everywhere, a mile to work and back in all weathers.
Trams along the main road from the station through the centre, packed at shift change.
Cabs from the rank by the station for those who can pay, and private carriages for those who own them.
Trains to the next towns along the line, cheap workmen's tickets before seven.
Mail and a few brave passengers by airship from the mast to the cities, weather permitting.
Everyone who can rides; a horse is how you get anywhere beyond the end of Main Street.
The stage to the railhead and the mining camps, twice a week, dusty, crowded and sometimes robbed.
Steamers and canal boats carrying coal, goods and a few passengers along the water.
A steam ferry across the harbour every half hour, a penny each way.
Downtown is walkable, and most people walk to the streetcar stop.
Electric streetcars from downtown out to the suburbs and the amusement park at the end of the line, a nickel a ride.
More families have a Ford every year, and the town has its first traffic policeman.
Jitney buses running the streetcar routes for a nickel, faster and less reliable.
The interurban electric railway to the next towns and the city, every hour.
A ferry across the bay and out to the islands, crowded with day-trippers in summer.
Downtown is easy to walk; the rest of town, less so.
Most people drive, and everyone has an opinion about the parking downtown.
Buses on a dozen routes, every twenty minutes on the main ones and hourly on the rest.
A light rail line from downtown through the university to the edge of town.
Docked bikes and scooters downtown and along the river path.
Rideshare cars for the nights out and the trips to the airport.
A ferry across the water and out to the islands, every hour in summer.
Corridors, ramps and stairs everywhere; a ring walks round in half an hour.
Big passenger lifts between the decks every few minutes, quieter at ship's night.
A tram along the ship from bow to stern, every few minutes by day.
Sky bridges and moving walkways link the towers; the old streets below are for walking.
A silent monorail looping the city every three minutes, high above the old streets.
Driverless shuttles summoned to any corner, cheap and slightly too polite.
Electric water taxis along the canals and across the harbour.
